Robust rate-of-change (RoC) estimates need many randomisation runs (`rand`), and these can take minutes per record.
This article explains when running `estimate_roc()` on several cores saves time, how to choose `use_parallel`, how to keep parallel results reproducible, and how to run RRatepol on a high-performance computing (HPC) cluster.

## Why use parallel computation

The processor of a computer has several cores, and each core can carry out one calculation at a time.
By default, R uses only one of them, so most of the computer stays idle while RRatepol works.

`estimate_roc()` repeats the same estimation many times, each time with a different random draw of sample ages and pollen counts, and then summarises all repetitions.
These randomisation runs do not depend on each other, so they can be shared out among several cores, much like dividing a pile of samples to be counted among several people.
The summary at the end is the same as with one core; only the waiting time is shorter.

This matters because reliable estimates need many randomisation runs: the [workflow example](workflow-example.html) recommends 10 000.
On a single core, this can keep the computer busy for a long time for each record, and the time multiplies with the number of records.
With several cores, the same work finishes in a fraction of that time (see the timing table below).

A typical call looks like this:

```{r quick-start, eval=FALSE}
# How many cores can R use on this computer?
parallelly::availableCores()

base::set.seed(900723)

data_roc <-
  RRatepol::estimate_roc(
    data_source_community =
      purrr::chuck(RRatepol::example_data, "pollen_data", 1),
    data_source_age =
      purrr::chuck(RRatepol::example_data, "sample_age", 1),
    age_uncertainty =
      purrr::chuck(RRatepol::example_data, "age_uncertainty", 1),
    rand = 10000,
    use_parallel = 4 # number of cores
  )
```

## What to watch for

- **Test first, then go parallel.** Try out settings with a small `rand` on a single core, where errors show up quickly and are easier to read. Switch on `use_parallel` for the final estimate with many runs.
- **Leave some cores free.** While RRatepol uses all cores, the computer can become slow, the fans loud, and a laptop battery drains fast. On a computer you also use for other work, give a number of cores (for example `use_parallel = 4`) rather than `use_parallel = TRUE`.
- **Watch the memory.** Each core works on its own copy of the data. If the computer runs out of memory or slows down sharply, use fewer cores.
- **Set a seed to make results repeatable.** With `set.seed()` before `estimate_roc()`, the results are identical whether you use one core or many. Without a seed, every call gives slightly different values, as expected from new randomisation runs. Report the seed, `rand`, and the RRatepol version with your results (see [Reproducible parallel results](#reproducible-parallel-results)).
- **Few runs gain little.** Starting the cores takes time, so with only a few randomisation runs, parallel computation saves little or nothing.
- **Shared computers and HPC clusters have rules.** On a server or cluster shared with others, use only the cores you have been given. On an HPC cluster, run RRatepol inside a job, never on the login node (see [Running RRatepol on an HPC cluster](#running-rratepol-on-an-hpc-cluster)).

## How parallel computation works in RRatepol

`estimate_roc()` repeats the whole estimation `rand` times.
In each randomisation run, it draws one age sequence from `age_uncertainty` (if supplied) and, with `standardise = TRUE`, a random subset of `n_individuals` from each working unit.
The runs are independent of each other, so they can be spread over several cores.

The argument `use_parallel` controls this:

- `FALSE` (default) or `1`: all runs on a single core.
- A whole number above 1: that many cores.
- `TRUE`: all cores available to the R session, as reported by `parallelly::availableCores()`.

With more than one core, `estimate_roc()` starts a local cluster of R worker processes on the same computer, sends the runs to the workers, and stops the cluster when the runs are finished, also when a run fails.

## When parallel computation pays off

Starting the workers and sending them the data takes time, so the time saved is small with few runs and grows with the number of runs.
The table below compares elapsed times for the first record of `example_data` with age uncertainty, Shepard's 5-term filter, moving-window binning, and taxa standardisation.

```{r benchmark-setup, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(RRatepol)

n_cores_available <-
  base::as.integer(parallelly::availableCores())

vec_cores <-
  c(1, 2, 4, 8)

vec_cores_tested <-
  vec_cores[vec_cores <= n_cores_available]

vec_rand <-
  c(10, 100, 500)

# Re-run the cached benchmark for a new package version or another number
#    of available cores
list_cache_key <-
  list(
    base::as.character(utils::packageVersion("RRatepol")),
    n_cores_available
  )
```

```{r benchmark, cache=TRUE, cache.extra=list_cache_key, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
data_benchmark <-
  tidyr::expand_grid(
    rand = vec_rand,
    n_cores = vec_cores_tested
  ) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    elapsed = purrr::map2_dbl(
      .x = rand,
      .y = n_cores,
      .f = ~ {
        base::set.seed(900723)

        time_run <-
          base::system.time(
            RRatepol::estimate_roc(
              data_source_community =
                purrr::chuck(example_data, "pollen_data", 1),
              data_source_age =
                purrr::chuck(example_data, "sample_age", 1),
              age_uncertainty =
                purrr::chuck(example_data, "age_uncertainty", 1),
              smooth_method = "shep",
              working_units = "MW",
              bin_size = 500,
              number_of_shifts = 5,
              standardise = TRUE,
              n_individuals = 150,
              rand = .x,
              use_parallel = .y,
              silent = TRUE
            )
          )

        purrr::chuck(time_run, "elapsed")
      }
    )
  )

benchmark_r_version <-
  base::R.version.string

benchmark_os <-
  purrr::chuck(base::Sys.info(), "sysname")
```

```{r benchmark-table}
data_benchmark_wide <-
  data_benchmark %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    n_cores = base::ifelse(
      test = n_cores == 1,
      yes = "1 core",
      no = base::paste(n_cores, "cores")
    ),
    elapsed = base::round(elapsed, 1)
  ) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_wider(
    names_from = n_cores,
    values_from = elapsed
  )

knitr::kable(
  data_benchmark_wide,
  caption = "Elapsed time (s) of estimate_roc() by number of cores"
)
```

```{r benchmark-summary, include=FALSE}
data_speed_up <-
  data_benchmark %>%
  dplyr::group_by(rand) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    relative_time = elapsed / elapsed[n_cores == 1]
  ) %>%
  dplyr::ungroup()

n_cores_max <-
  base::max(vec_cores_tested)

relative_time_small <-
  data_speed_up %>%
  dplyr::filter(
    rand == base::min(vec_rand),
    n_cores == n_cores_max
  ) %>%
  dplyr::pull(relative_time)

relative_time_large <-
  data_speed_up %>%
  dplyr::filter(
    rand == base::max(vec_rand),
    n_cores == n_cores_max
  ) %>%
  dplyr::pull(relative_time)
```

The times were measured on `r benchmark_os` with `r benchmark_r_version` and `r n_cores_available` available cores; they depend on the computer and on its load at the time.
With `r base::min(vec_rand)` runs, `r n_cores_max` cores needed `r base::round(100 * relative_time_small)` % of the single-core time.
With `r base::max(vec_rand)` runs, they needed `r base::round(100 * relative_time_large)` %.
Adding cores shortens the time less than proportionally, because starting the workers and collecting their results do not get faster with more cores.

In practice:

- For quick checks with few runs, the default `use_parallel = FALSE` saves little time compared with several cores.
- For final estimates with hundreds or thousands of runs, use several cores.
- More cores give diminishing returns; leave some cores free for other work on a shared computer.

## Choosing `use_parallel`

`use_parallel = TRUE` uses all cores available to the R session.
`parallelly::availableCores()` respects the cores allocated to a job by an HPC scheduler (for example SLURM, PBS, or SGE), the limits of a container, and the option `mc.cores`, so RRatepol does not start more workers than the session may use.
To see how many cores `use_parallel = TRUE` would use, run:

```{r available-cores, eval=FALSE}
parallelly::availableCores()
```

A number, such as `use_parallel = 4`, sets the number of cores explicitly.
This is useful on a shared computer, where `use_parallel = TRUE` would take all available cores.
If only one core is available, `use_parallel = TRUE` runs on a single core without starting a cluster.

## Reproducible parallel results

Each randomisation run has its own random-number stream, created from the random-number generator of the main R session before the runs start.
A run draws the same random numbers whether it is computed in the main session or on any worker.
Calling `set.seed()` before `estimate_roc()` therefore gives identical results on a single core and on any number of cores, with or without progress output (`silent`).
The chunk below runs the same estimation on one core and on two cores:

```{r reproducibility, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
list_roc_parallel <-
  purrr::map(
    .x = list(FALSE, 2),
    .f = ~ {
      base::set.seed(900723)

      RRatepol::estimate_roc(
        data_source_community =
          purrr::chuck(example_data, "pollen_data", 1),
        data_source_age =
          purrr::chuck(example_data, "sample_age", 1),
        age_uncertainty =
          purrr::chuck(example_data, "age_uncertainty", 1),
        smooth_method = "shep",
        working_units = "MW",
        bin_size = 500,
        number_of_shifts = 5,
        standardise = TRUE,
        n_individuals = 150,
        rand = 10,
        use_parallel = .x,
        silent = TRUE
      )
    }
  )

base::identical(
  purrr::chuck(list_roc_parallel, 1),
  purrr::chuck(list_roc_parallel, 2)
)
```

For results that others should reproduce exactly, report the seed, `rand`, and the RRatepol version.
The number of cores does not need to be reported, because it does not change the results.
Versions before 1.4.0 gave different random draws for the same seed; to reproduce results of an earlier version, install that version.

## Memory

Each worker is a separate R process that loads RRatepol and receives its own copy of the data for the runs it computes.
Memory use therefore grows with the number of cores.
For large records or many cores, check the memory available to the session (on an HPC cluster, the memory requested for the job) before increasing `use_parallel`.

## Running RRatepol on an HPC cluster

The cluster that `estimate_roc()` starts runs on one computer.
On an HPC cluster, this means one node: request several cores on a single node for one job.
The examples below use the SLURM scheduler; the directives differ for other schedulers, and the module names, partitions, and resource limits depend on the site.

### One record on one node

An R script `estimate_roc_record.R`:

```{r hpc-single-script, eval=FALSE}
library(RRatepol)

base::set.seed(900723)

data_roc <-
  RRatepol::estimate_roc(
    data_source_community =
      purrr::chuck(example_data, "pollen_data", 1),
    data_source_age =
      purrr::chuck(example_data, "sample_age", 1),
    age_uncertainty =
      purrr::chuck(example_data, "age_uncertainty", 1),
    smooth_method = "shep",
    working_units = "MW",
    bin_size = 500,
    number_of_shifts = 5,
    standardise = TRUE,
    n_individuals = 150,
    rand = 10000,
    use_parallel = TRUE,
    silent = TRUE
  )

base::saveRDS(
  object = data_roc,
  file = "roc_record_1.rds"
)
```

A job script `estimate_roc_record.sh`, submitted with `sbatch estimate_roc_record.sh`:

```{bash hpc-single-job, eval=FALSE}
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=rratepol
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --mem=8G
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00

# Load R as provided on your cluster
module load R

Rscript estimate_roc_record.R
```

`--cpus-per-task` sets the number of cores of the job, and `use_parallel = TRUE` uses exactly these cores.
Adjust the memory and time requests to your data and the rules of your cluster.

### Many records with a job array

For many records, it is usually more efficient to run one record per job on a single core and let the scheduler run many jobs at the same time.
A job array starts the same script many times, each with a different task number.

An R script `estimate_roc_array.R` that selects the record by the task number:

```{r hpc-array-script, eval=FALSE}
library(RRatepol)

index_record <-
  base::as.integer(base::Sys.getenv("SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID"))

base::set.seed(900723)

data_roc <-
  RRatepol::estimate_roc(
    data_source_community =
      purrr::chuck(example_data, "pollen_data", index_record),
    data_source_age =
      purrr::chuck(example_data, "sample_age", index_record),
    age_uncertainty =
      purrr::chuck(example_data, "age_uncertainty", index_record),
    smooth_method = "shep",
    working_units = "MW",
    bin_size = 500,
    number_of_shifts = 5,
    standardise = TRUE,
    n_individuals = 150,
    rand = 10000,
    use_parallel = FALSE,
    silent = TRUE
  )

base::saveRDS(
  object = data_roc,
  file = base::paste0("roc_record_", index_record, ".rds")
)
```

A job script `estimate_roc_array.sh` with one task per record of `example_data`:

```{bash hpc-array-job, eval=FALSE}
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=rratepol-array
#SBATCH --array=1-4
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1
#SBATCH --mem=2G
#SBATCH --time=08:00:00

module load R

Rscript estimate_roc_array.R
```

With your own data, set `--array` to the number of records and read each record from a file in the R script.
Each task uses the same seed; because the tasks process different records, the results do not depend on each other.
If single jobs take too long, combine both approaches: a job array with a few cores per task and `use_parallel = TRUE`.
